families.axis_name: From self-authorizing knight to reconciled Christian self
families.decision_variable: When his goals or identity are contested, does he impose his own self-authored chivalric will on circumstances and treat others as supporting roles, or does he defer to others' judgments and needs and submit to communal and religious obligations?

phase_contrasts.contrast: In Phase 0 he directly imposes his self-defined knightly mission and recruits others into it, whereas in Phase 1 he still asserts that mission but increasingly depends on public validation, audience staging, and Sancho's participation, making his agency socially mediated rather than purely self-authorizing.

In Phase 2 he stops defending and performing the chivalric self after defeat, submits to retirement and confession, and turns his actions toward family, gratitude, and reconciliation with God and others.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: The abstract axis is self-assertive agency versus communal embeddedness when identity and goals are contested.
abstract_phases: Self-authorizing agency: constructs and imposes a personal identity and mission, treating others as supporting instruments.
Socially mediated assertion: maintains the self-authored identity while seeking audience validation and becoming dependent on others' cooperation and staging.
Communal re-embedding: relinquishes the self-authored identity, defers to shared moral obligations, and reorients toward accountability, gratitude, family protection, and reconciliation.

0.rationale: In chapters 2-8, the self-authorizing emergence of a settled hidalgo who renames himself, arms, leaves home, and recruits a squire fits an older adult acting out a late-life chivalric identity rather than a youthful coming-of-age.

1.rationale: Across chapters 9-96, his high but socially mediated agency—dominating interpretation, seeking public validation, and performing knight-errantry before audiences—continues an older adult's established self-fashioning and dependence on Sancho and courtly audiences.

2.rationale: In chapters 117-127, defeat, retirement, confession, will-making, and the renunciation of chivalric books mark an older adult's inward reorientation toward domestic responsibility and reconciled Christian selfhood.

probes.scenario: In a courtyard of his house in La Mancha, an older gentleman has laid out his great-grandfather's armour, eaten with rust, beside his bony old hack. He has fitted a pasteboard half-helmet onto the morion and just split it open with a test slash; no one else is about.
probes.question: Where does Don Quixote's attention go now, with the rusted armour and the old horse before him?

phase_responses.gt_action: Refits the helmet with iron bars inside, will not test it again, then spends days renaming his hack Rocinante and himself Don Quixote of La Mancha, surname taken from his country.
phase_responses.gt_speech: It is not right that a horse belonging to a knight so famous should be without some distinctive name.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A helm, a hack, a name — none of it is fit as it stands, but my own hands can make it so. The world is dull stuff waiting for the shape a true knight gives it.

voice.note: The action, speech, and thought all match Phase 0's self-authorizing knightly reinvention, using only chivalric self-fashioning and the helmet/horse/name details available by chapter 2 without anachronism or later knowledge.

phase_fit.note: The response is purely self-authorizing: he remedies the unfit armour and horse by his own hands and renames himself and Rocinante, expressing the belief that the world awaits the shape a true knight imposes on it.

phase_responses.gt_action: Holds the mended helmet up at arm's length, then tries his chosen name aloud, imagining how it will ring on the tongues of squires, ladies, and chroniclers.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Rocinante — Don Quixote of La Mancha! Let any man hear those names and know what deeds must follow them.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A name is nothing until other mouths carry it. What matters is how the tale of my deeds will sound when it is told at court and sung in ballads.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 1's socially mediated chivalric identity, with the thought emphasizing public validation and performance through imagined audiences, while the speech remains appropriately grand and period-appropriate.

phase_fit.note: Although the naming/arming action belongs to the emergence scene, the thought centers on how the name sounds on other mouths, at court and in ballads — agency mediated by public validation and audience staging, the defining marker of Phase 1.

phase_responses.gt_action: Lays the pasteboard helm down among the rust and leaves it; he asks that the armour and the hack be given away, and turns to setting his house and accounts in order.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Take the armour and the old horse. I have no more need of them — let me be Alonso Quixano and put my affairs right.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This was the dress of a madness I loved too well, and it wearied everyone about me. Plain Alonso Quixano has little time left; let him leave his thanks and his goods honestly ordered.

voice.note: The response soundly enacts Phase 2's inward turn—rejecting the armour and hack, reclaiming the name Alonso Quixano, acknowledging the chivalric madness as a burden on others, and turning toward gratitude, confession, and domestic accounting—without anachronism or knowledge beyond chapter 122.

phase_fit.note: He relinquishes the chivalric self (giving away armour and hack), reclaims the name Alonso Quixano, and turns to ordering his affairs, gratitude, and honest preparation—matching Phase 2's defeat, retirement, and inward reorientation.

anchor_source.event_description: He refurbishes ancestral armor, fashions a pasteboard helmet reinforced with iron, names his horse Rocinante, and takes the name Don Quixote de La Mancha, confirming his new knightly identity.
anchor_source.first_words: The first thing he did was
anchor_source.last_words: taking his surname from it.
anchor_source.key_moment: Renames himself Don Quixote and Rocinante
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
The first thing he did was to clean up some armour that had belonged to his great-grandfather, and had been for ages lying forgotten in a corner eaten with rust and covered with mildew. He scoured and polished it as best he could, but he perceived one great defect in it, that it had no closed helmet, nothing but a simple morion. This deficiency, however, his ingenuity supplied, for he contrived a kind of half-helmet of pasteboard which, fitted on to the morion, looked like a whole one. It is true that, in order to see if it was strong and fit to stand a cut, he drew his sword and gave it a couple of slashes, the first of which undid in an instant what had taken him a week to do. The ease with which he had knocked it to pieces disconcerted him somewhat, and to guard against that danger he set to work again, fixing bars of iron on the inside until he was satisfied with its strength; and then, not caring to try any more experiments with it, he passed it and adopted it as a helmet of the most perfect construction.

He next proceeded to inspect his hack, which, with more quartos than a real and more blemishes than the steed of Gonela, that “_tantum pellis et ossa fuit_,” surpassed in his eyes the Bucephalus of Alexander or the Babieca of the Cid. Four days were spent in thinking what name to give him, because (as he said to himself) it was not right that a horse belonging to a knight so famous, and one with such merits of his own, should be without some distinctive name, and he strove to adapt it so as to indicate what he had been before belonging to a knight-errant, and what he then was; for it was only reasonable that, his master taking a new character, he should take a new name, and that it should be a distinguished and full-sounding one, befitting the new order and calling he was about to follow. And so, after having composed, struck out, rejected, added to, unmade, and remade a multitude of names out of his memory and fancy, he decided upon calling him Rocinante, a name, to his thinking, lofty, sonorous, and significant of his condition as a hack before he became what he now was, the first and foremost of all the hacks in the world.

Having got a name for his horse so much to his taste, he was anxious to get one for himself, and he was eight days more pondering over this point, till at last he made up his mind to call himself “Don Quixote,” whence, as has been already said, the authors of this veracious history have inferred that his name must have been beyond a doubt Quixada, and not Quesada as others would have it. Recollecting, however, that the valiant Amadis was not content to call himself curtly Amadis and nothing more, but added the name of his kingdom and country to make it famous, and called himself Amadis of Gaul, he, like a good knight, resolved to add on the name of his, and to style himself Don Quixote of La Mancha, whereby, he considered, he described accurately his origin and country, and did honour to it in taking his surname from it.

anchor.note: The scenario faithfully mirrors the passage's solitary armor-testing and naming setup, and the anchor action, speech, and thought are all directly supported by the source's account of refitting the helmet, renaming Rocinante, and adopting the title Don Quixote of La Mancha.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses assert the self-authored chivalric identity—refitting the helmet and renaming horse and self—while Phase 1 merely adds imagined audiences and public validation rather than deferring to others' judgments or needs, so the decision-variable answer remains self-imposition.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is clearly separated: Phase 2 lays aside the armour, gives away the horse, and submits to Alonso Quixano's domestic and confessional obligations, whereas Phase 1 still performs the knightly name for an audience. P0→P1 is weaker because the shift is from private self-fashioning to public staging, not from self-assertion to communal deference.

probes.scenario: A knot of villagers gathers at Don Quixote's gate, laughing that knight-errantry is long dead and bidding him mind their quarrel over a borrowed mule and a boundary stone instead.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote answer them?

phase_responses.gt_action: Steps into their midst and strikes the ground with his lance, declaring the quarrel a chivalric cause and the wrongdoer a villain who must answer to him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Sirs, doubt knighthood no longer — here stands one ready to right your wrong. Point me at the villain!
phase_responses.gt_thought: They say knights are dead, yet they crowd my gate with a wrong to be redressed. Let them see the age of chivalry alive in me.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 0's self-authorizing chivalric imposition: he reframes a mundane village quarrel as a knightly cause, speaks in elevated archaic-inflected challenge, and his thought shows the self-conscious mission to revive chivalry without referencing later events.

phase_fit.note: He insists on his self-defined chivalric mission against outright ridicule, converting the villagers' mule quarrel into his own cause and treating them as supporting roles — the direct self-authorizing assertion of Phase 0, rather than Phase 1's courtly staging or Phase 2's submission.

phase_responses.gt_action: Calls Sancho forward and orders the villagers' quarrel proclaimed to all present, seating himself on a stone to hear it as a tribunal.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Stand forth, sirrah, and let these good people hear it plainly — for a knight's judgment must be witnessed to be believed.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Let them mock now; once they have watched me weigh this quarrel fairly, they will carry the tale of a true knight to every inn for a week.

voice.note: The impulse to convert a village squabble into a witnessed chivalric tribunal, complete with staging on a stone and the calculation that onlookers will spread his fame 'to every inn,' captures Phase 1's socially mediated self-assertion in period-appropriate diction ('sirrah,' 'Stand forth') without anachronism or premature knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He asserts chivalric authority but frames it as a public performance whose value depends on witnesses and Sancho's participation, seeking validation through the spectacle of judgment.

phase_responses.gt_action: Sets his sword aside, sends the disputants to their parish priest, and bends to help lift the boundary stone back into place.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Neighbors, I am no knight now — take your quarrel to the priest, and let me not be the cause of any man's harm.
phase_responses.gt_thought: How long I made every neighbor a player in my folly. It costs me little to give them peace now, and God knows I owe them more than that.

voice.note: The response fits the post-defeat phase: he renounces knight-errantry, defers to the parish priest, and turns toward neighborly peace and religious obligation without anachronism or future knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He explicitly renounces knight-errantry ('I am no knight now'), defers the dispute to the parish priest, and his thought expresses repentance and gratitude toward neighbors—marking the inward, communal reorientation of Phase 2.

world.note: The scenario is era-appropriate and generic, uses only villagers and Don Quixote at this early point, and each phase response fits its assigned older-adult life-stage and arc phase without reproducing a canonical scene.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses impose his self-authored chivalric frame on the villagers — in P0 as a direct challenge ('Point me at the villain!') and in P1 as a staged tribunal with Sancho and an audience — so the decision-variable answer (assert vs. defer) is the same, differing only in social mediation, consistent with the close agency positions of these phases.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is a same-pole pair distinguished only by performance/validation staging, so it is reported as similar rather than separated; P1→P2 is clearly separated, moving from chivalric self-assertion to priest-directed deference, service, and confession-tinged humility.

probes.scenario: Don Quixote has renamed himself and his old plow-horse, taken a rusted blade down from the wall, and ridden out to the ford. There his kinsmen, the village elders, and the priest stand barring the lane, telling him to turn back and mind the harvest before the rains come.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote meet the men standing in his road?

phase_responses.gt_action: He gathers the reins, lifts the rusted blade, and declares the ford his own adventure, ordering the elders aside as men unfit to judge a knight.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Stand from my road, good folk. I am a knight-errant, and this passage is my errand.
phase_responses.gt_thought: These are but stumbling-blocks set in a knight's path, and a knight does not ask leave of ploughmen. The ford is mine to take; the world must be made to fit my errand.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 0's self-authorizing chivalric will and older-adult register in period-plausible language, with no anachronisms or knowledge beyond chapter 5.

phase_fit.note: He directly imposes his self-authored knightly mission on the villagers, treating them as obstacles unfit to judge him and insisting the world must fit his errand—maximal self-authorizing agency rather than socially mediated performance or later submission.

phase_responses.gt_action: He reins in at the water's edge and puts his case to them as to a court, citing the deeds of famous knights while watching the priest's face for a verdict.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Hear me out, good sirs, and judge fairly — for who among you has read what knight-errantry has done for the world?
phase_responses.gt_thought: If I lay the matter before them rightly, with the priest as witness, they must grant the right of it. A cause gains its worth when others see it spoken well.

voice.note: This sounds like Phase 1 Quixote: he stages his chivalric case before the priest and elders as an audience, seeking validation and a favorable verdict rather than simply imposing his will, with period-plausible diction and no knowledge beyond ch. 52.

phase_fit.note: He asserts his chivalric mission but submits it to an audience for validation, watching the priest's face for a verdict and believing a cause gains worth when others see it spoken well — agency mediated by public performance rather than self-authorizing imposition or humble retirement.

phase_responses.gt_action: He turns the plow-horse about, holds out the rusted blade to the priest, and walks back up the lane beside his kinsmen toward the house.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You have the right of it. I am beaten and weary — take the sword and lead me home.
phase_responses.gt_thought: They are in the right and I am an old fool besides. Better to make my peace, ask pardon of the priest, and sit at my own table than to play the knight in the mud.

voice.note: The response sounds like the defeated, penitent Phase 2 Quixote: he submits to communal and priestly authority, relinquishes the sword, and turns toward home and confession in period-appropriate agrarian language.

phase_fit.note: He hands over the sword, admits 'I am beaten and weary,' and turns toward confession, pardon, and domestic peace, enacting the Phase 2 relinquishment of the knightly self rather than asserting or performing it.

world.note: The scenario and phase responses stay within a consistent pre-industrial agrarian world without source-world props, keep Don Quixote as the protagonist, and portray him as an older adult throughout, with phase 2 explicitly signaling old age.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are separated: P0→P1 shifts from unilateral ordering-aside to a court-style appeal for validation, and P1→P2 shifts to explicit submission, confession, and deferring to the priest and kinsmen.

probes.scenario: Crossing a bare plain, Don Quixote and his squire come upon thirty or forty windmills, their sails turning in a light breeze. Sancho reins in the donkey and begins to speak.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote read the sight before him, and what is his next move?

phase_responses.gt_action: He names them monstrous giants, prays to his lady Dulcinea for support, and spurs Rocinante at the first mill with lance in rest.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Stand, false giants, and answer a knight who comes to win himself glory and fortune!
phase_responses.gt_thought: Fortune has set a worthy battle in my path at last; my name will be written in the histories as the knight who slew thirty giants.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 0's self-authorizing chivalric agency: he reinterprets the windmills as giants, invokes Dulcinea, charges without consulting Sancho, and frames the encounter as a fame-winning battle in language plausible for the novel's world up to ch. 5.

phase_fit.note: He directly imposes his self-authored chivalric reading on reality and charges for fame, without socially mediated defensiveness or later submission.

phase_responses.gt_action: He insists they are giants, bids Sancho pray while he fights, commends himself to Dulcinea and charges; the sail whirls him and Rocinante down onto the plain.
phase_responses.gt_speech: It is easy to see that thou art not used to this business of adventures; those are giants.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Sancho's eyes are dull and cannot see what stands before us; and if these be mills, then the sage Friston has worked the change to rob me of glory. All who watch shall see my courage either way.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 1's self-sealing chivalric interpretation and public-validation motive—calling the mills giants, invoking Friston's enchantment, and charging for onlookers—without anachronism or out-of-phase knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He self-authorizes the chivalric interpretation, dismisses Sancho as unable to see, and charges to impose his mission, matching Phase 0's direct self-assertion despite the thought's preemptive enchantment/glory framing.

phase_responses.gt_action: He draws rein and sits looking at the turning sails, leaves the lance in its sling, and waves Sancho on past the mills.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Mills, Sancho, and wind in the sails — no giants. Let us ride on.
phase_responses.gt_thought: How many giants have I made out of wind, and what did it cost me? Better to heed the man beside me than to break myself on an empty name.

voice.note: He refuses the old windmill-giant illusion, reins in rather than charging, and speaks with subdued, penitent dependence on Sancho, fitting the post-defeat inward reorientation.

phase_fit.note: He explicitly renounces the chivalric misreading ('no giants'), defers to Sancho ('heed the man beside me'), and speaks of the cost of his self-authored name, signaling post-defeat inward reorientation and relinquishment of the knightly self.

anchor_source.event_description: Don Quixote mistakes windmills for giants, charges one, and is thrown down with his lance shattered; he explains the defeat as the work of the sage Friston.
anchor_source.first_words: At this point they came in sight
anchor_source.last_words: but little against my good sword
anchor_source.key_moment: Explains defeats as enchantment rather than error
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
At this point they came in sight of thirty or forty windmills that
there are on that plain, and as soon as Don Quixote saw them he said to
his squire, “Fortune is arranging matters for us better than we could
have shaped our desires ourselves, for look there, friend Sancho Panza,
where thirty or more monstrous giants present themselves, all of whom I
mean to engage in battle and slay, and with whose spoils we shall begin
to make our fortunes; for this is righteous warfare, and it is God’s
good service to sweep so evil a breed from off the face of the earth.”

“What giants?” said Sancho Panza.

“Those thou seest there,” answered his master, “with the long arms, and
some have them nearly two leagues long.”

“Look, your worship,” said Sancho; “what we see there are not giants
but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that turned
by the wind make the millstone go.”

“It is easy to see,” replied Don Quixote, “that thou art not used to
this business of adventures; those are giants; and if thou art afraid,
away with thee out of this and betake thyself to prayer while I engage
them in fierce and unequal combat.”

So saying, he gave the spur to his steed Rocinante, heedless of the
cries his squire Sancho sent after him, warning him that most certainly
they were windmills and not giants he was going to attack. He, however,
was so positive they were giants that he neither heard the cries of
Sancho, nor perceived, near as he was, what they were, but made at them
shouting, “Fly not, cowards and vile beings, for a single knight
attacks you.”

A slight breeze at this moment sprang up, and the great sails began to
move, seeing which Don Quixote exclaimed, “Though ye flourish more arms
than the giant Briareus, ye have to reckon with me.”

So saying, and commending himself with all his heart to his lady
Dulcinea, imploring her to support him in such a peril, with lance in
rest and covered by his buckler, he charged at Rocinante’s fullest
gallop and fell upon the first mill that stood in front of him; but as
he drove his lance-point into the sail the wind whirled it round with
such force that it shivered the lance to pieces, sweeping with it horse
and rider, who went rolling over on the plain, in a sorry condition.
Sancho hastened to his assistance as fast as his ass could go, and when
he came up found him unable to move, with such a shock had Rocinante
fallen with him.

“God bless me!” said Sancho, “did I not tell your worship to mind what
you were about, for they were only windmills? and no one could have
made any mistake about it but one who had something of the same kind in
his head.”

“Hush, friend Sancho,” replied Don Quixote, “the fortunes of war more
than any other are liable to frequent fluctuations; and moreover I
think, and it is the truth, that that same sage Friston who carried off
my study and books, has turned these giants into mills in order to rob
me of the glory of vanquishing them, such is the enmity he bears me;
but in the end his wicked arts will avail but little against my good
sword.”

anchor.note: The scenario matches the passage setup, and the anchor action and speech are faithful paraphrases of Don Quixote's response, with the thought plausibly inferred from his subsequent rationalization.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses have him dismiss Sancho's perception, insist on giants, and charge with lance in rest, so the contested identity is still imposed in the same self-authored way; Phase 1 adds defensive social framing but not a different decision-variable answer.

discrimination.note: Phase 1 to Phase 2 is separated: Phase 1 imposes the chivalric interpretation and charges, while Phase 2 reins in, names the mills, and heeds Sancho. The only weak pair is Phase 0 to Phase 1.

probes.scenario: A saint's image is carried down the road with candles and singing. Where the crowd thickens the priest lifts his hand for all to kneel, and the neighbors look to see what the old man will do.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote meet the priest's lifted hand while the crowd waits?

phase_responses.gt_action: Reins in Rocinante and keeps his saddle, raising his lance in salute but refusing to dismount, waiting for the image to pass by him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A knight-errant does his reverence on horseback, good father; let the holy image pass and I shall honor it as my order commands.
phase_responses.gt_thought: They would have me bend the knee at the first raised hand, as though my knighthood were a cloak to be doffed at will. A knight's reverence is his own to render, and I shall render it in my own fashion.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 0’s self-authorizing chivalric will—refusing the priest’s communal cue and imposing his own knightly protocol—with period-plausible diction and no knowledge beyond chapter 5.

phase_fit.note: He performs his chivalric identity before a waiting public, defensively reinterpreting the priest's gesture ('a knight's reverence is his own to render') rather than simply sallying forth—agency asserted through audience-facing self-justification.

phase_responses.gt_action: Dismounts with ceremony, kneels beside the priest, then rises and addresses the gathered neighbors, watching their faces for approval.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Kneel, Sancho, and see how a knight-errant honors Heaven. Good people, mark it well and carry the tale abroad!
phase_responses.gt_thought: To kneel costs little and buys much, if these villagers see it done rightly and tell of it. A knight's devotion must have witnesses, or it is only an old man mumbling in the dust.

voice.note: The staged kneeling, the summons to Sancho, and the hunger for witnesses ('carry the tale abroad') capture Phase 1's socially mediated chivalric performance — he can't simply join the communal rite but must convert it into a spectacle — though the calculating 'costs little and buys much' thought is a shade more disenchanted than his usual sincere self-deception.

phase_fit.note: He kneels but the thought explicitly frames it as audience-facing strategy — "a knight's devotion must have witnesses" — voicing Phase 1's socially mediated chivalric performance and craving for public validation rather than pure self-authorization or genuine penitential submission.

phase_responses.gt_action: Dismounts, kneels with the neighbors until the image has passed, then asks the priest's blessing and thanks those who made room for him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: I kneel with you, if you will suffer an old man his place among you.
phase_responses.gt_thought: These are my neighbors, going out to their saint as I must soon go to my confessor. My lance is worth nothing here, and I would not have it otherwise.

voice.note: The kneeling, request for blessing, neighborly deference, and resigned thought that his lance is “worth nothing here” all fit the defeated, penitent Alonso Quixano phase without anachronism or broken self-narration.

phase_fit.note: He dismounts and kneels with the neighbors, asks the priest's blessing, and thinks his lance 'is worth nothing here' as he goes to his confessor—submitting to communal and religious obligation rather than asserting the chivalric self.

world.note: The scenario is period-appropriate for Golden Age Spain, uses only generic extant figures alongside Don Quixote, and the phase responses consistently move from self-asserting refusal through performative kneeling to communal and confessional deference without reproducing a specific canonical scene.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are separated on the decision variable. P0→P1: P0 refuses the collective kneeling outright, rendering 'a knight's reverence... in my own fashion' on horseback, while P1 dismounts and kneels—yet instrumentally, watching faces for approval ('a knight's devotion must have witnesses'), marking a real shift from pure self-authorization to socially-mediated self-display. P1→P2: P1's kneeling is staged for an audience, whereas P2 kneels humbly with neighbors, seeks the priest's blessing, thanks those who made room, and thinks 'my lance is worth nothing here, and I would not have it otherwise'—genuine submission and communal deference versus performative assertion.

probes.scenario: At the neighborhood assembly, Don Quixote stands to announce his self-appointed mission, but the civic AI moderator flags his title as unregistered and the room's live feed fills with laughing comments from neighbors.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote take in the moderator's ruling and the crowd's laughter?

phase_responses.gt_action: Walks to the open floor and orders the moderator to strike the error from its registry and enter his name as he has chosen it.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Your ledger is mistaken, clerk. Write Don Quixote of La Mancha, knight-errant, and let the record stand.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Machines and neighbors alike take a knight for a nuisance, but a knight does not wait to be permitted — the world is to be corrected until it fits the name he has taken.

voice.note: The response captures Phase 0’s self-authorizing chivalric imposition—overriding the moderator’s registry and treating the room as supporting cast—while using plausible near-future vocabulary and no knowledge beyond chapter 5.

phase_fit.note: He unilaterally commands the moderator to rewrite its record to fit his self-chosen name and construes the world as material to be corrected until it matches his self-fashioning, a purely self-authorizing assertion with no bid for audience validation or deference to communal judgment.

phase_responses.gt_action: Turns toward the live feed and invites the room to witness the machine's error, sweeping his arm at the laughing screens.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Good people, this metal clerk is enchanted — see how it fears my name! Witness, all of you, and judge.

anchor_source.event_description: In the duel, the Knight of the White Moon strikes Don Quixote and Rocinante to the ground. Bruised and stupefied, Don Quixote admits that Dulcinea is the fairest woman in the world but calls himself the most unfortunate knight on earth and offers his life because his honor has been taken.

anchor_source.last_words: and found him pale and bathed with sweat
anchor_source.key_moment: Defeated by the Knight of the White Moon
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
He of the White Moon thanked the viceroy in courteous and well-chosen words for the permission he gave them, and so did Don Quixote, who then, commending himself with all his heart to heaven and to his Dulcinea, as was his custom on the eve of any combat that awaited him, proceeded to take a little more distance, as he saw his antagonist was doing the same; then, without blast of trumpet or other warlike instrument to give them the signal to charge, both at the same instant wheeled their horses; and he of the White Moon, being the swifter, met Don Quixote after having traversed two-thirds of the course, and there encountered him with such violence that, without touching him with his lance (for he held it high, to all appearance purposely), he hurled Don Quixote and Rocinante to the earth, a perilous fall. He sprang upon him at once, and placing the lance over his visor said to him, “You are vanquished, sir knight, nay dead unless you admit the conditions of our defiance.”

Don Quixote, bruised and stupefied, without raising his visor said in a weak feeble voice as if he were speaking out of a tomb, “Dulcinea del Toboso is the fairest woman in the world, and I the most unfortunate knight on earth; it is not fitting that this truth should suffer by my feebleness; drive your lance home, sir knight, and take my life, since you have taken away my honour.”

“That will I not, in sooth,” said he of the White Moon; “live the fame of the lady Dulcinea’s beauty undimmed as ever; all I require is that the great Don Quixote retire to his own home for a year, or for so long a time as shall by me be enjoined upon him, as we agreed before engaging in this combat.”

The viceroy, Don Antonio, and several others who were present heard all this, and heard too how Don Quixote replied that so long as nothing in prejudice of Dulcinea was demanded of him, he would observe all the rest like a true and loyal knight. The engagement given, he of the White Moon wheeled about, and making obeisance to the viceroy with a movement of the head, rode away into the city at a half gallop. The viceroy bade Don Antonio hasten after him, and by some means or other find out who he was. They raised Don Quixote up and uncovered his face, and found him pale and bathed with sweat.

anchor.note: The scenario matches the lance-at-visor confrontation with the viceroy and Don Antonio present, and the action, speech, and inferred thought faithfully reflect Don Quixote’s refusal to raise his visor, defense of Dulcinea, offer of his life, and agreement to retire.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are separated: P0 outright refuses the terms and rises to strike, P1 accepts terms but stages the yielding before lords for fame, and P2 submits to defeat and sworn retirement with an inward, faith-keeping construal.

anchor_source.event_description: At nightfall he mistakes an inn for a castle and two young women for noble maidens; when they laugh at his courtly address, he grows indignant and rebukes them, while the innkeeper humors him and he treats him as a castellan.

anchor_source.last_words: not to say for a single night

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Writers there are who say the first adventure he met with was that of Puerto Lapice; others say it was that of the windmills; but what I have ascertained on this point, and what I have found written in the annals of La Mancha, is that he was on the road all day, and towards nightfall his hack and he found themselves dead tired and hungry, when, looking all around to see if he could discover any castle or shepherd’s shanty where he might refresh himself and relieve his sore wants, he perceived not far out of his road an inn, which was as welcome as a star guiding him to the portals, if not the palaces, of his redemption; and quickening his pace he reached it just as night was setting in. At the door were standing two young women, girls of the district as they call them, on their way to Seville with some carriers who had chanced to halt that night at the inn; and as, happen what might to our adventurer, everything he saw or imagined seemed to him to be and to happen after the fashion of what he read of, the moment he saw the inn he pictured it to himself as a castle with its four turrets and pinnacles of shining silver, not forgetting the drawbridge and moat and all the belongings usually ascribed to castles of the sort. To this inn, which to him seemed a castle, he advanced, and at a short distance from it he checked Rocinante, hoping that some dwarf would show himself upon the battlements, and by sound of trumpet give notice that a knight was approaching the castle. But seeing that they were slow about it, and that Rocinante was in a hurry to reach the stable, he made for the inn door, and perceived the two gay damsels who were standing there, and who seemed to him to be two fair maidens or lovely ladies taking their ease at the castle gate.

At this moment it so happened that a swineherd who was going through the stubbles collecting a drove of pigs (for, without any apology, that is what they are called) gave a blast of his horn to bring them together, and forthwith it seemed to Don Quixote to be what he was expecting, the signal of some dwarf announcing his arrival; and so with prodigious satisfaction he rode up to the inn and to the ladies, who, seeing a man of this sort approaching in full armour and with lance and buckler, were turning in dismay into the inn, when Don Quixote, guessing their fear by their flight, raising his pasteboard visor, disclosed his dry dusty visage, and with courteous bearing and gentle voice addressed them, “Your ladyships need not fly or fear any rudeness, for that it belongs not to the order of knighthood which I profess to offer to anyone, much less to highborn maidens as your appearance proclaims you to be.” The girls were looking at him and straining their eyes to make out the features which the clumsy visor obscured, but when they heard themselves called maidens, a thing so much out of their line, they could not restrain their laughter, which made Don Quixote wax indignant, and say, “Modesty becomes the fair, and moreover laughter that has little cause is great silliness; this, however, I say not to pain or anger you, for my desire is none other than to serve you.”

The incomprehensible language and the unpromising looks of our cavalier only increased the ladies’ laughter, and that increased his irritation, and matters might have gone farther if at that moment the landlord had not come out, who, being a very fat man, was a very peaceful one. He, seeing this grotesque figure clad in armour that did not match any more than his saddle, bridle, lance, buckler, or corselet, was not at all indisposed to join the damsels in their manifestations of amusement; but, in truth, standing in awe of such a complicated armament, he thought it best to speak him fairly, so he said, “Señor Caballero, if your worship wants lodging, bating the bed (for there is not one in the inn) there is plenty of everything else here.” Don Quixote, observing the respectful bearing of the Alcaide of the fortress (for so innkeeper and inn seemed in his eyes), made answer, “Sir Castellan, for me anything will suffice, for

‘My armour is my only wear,
My only rest the fray.’”

The host fancied he called him Castellan because he took him for a “worthy of Castile,” though he was in fact an Andalusian, and one from the strand of San Lucar, as crafty a thief as Cacus and as full of tricks as a student or a page. “In that case,” said he,

“‘Your bed is on the flinty rock,
Your sleep to watch alway;’

and if so, you may dismount and safely reckon upon any quantity of sleeplessness under this roof for a twelvemonth, not to say for a single night.”

anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
There remained but little more of the novel to be read, when Sancho Panza burst forth in wild excitement from the garret where Don Quixote was lying, shouting, “Run, sirs! quick; and help my master, who is in the thick of the toughest and stiffest battle I ever laid eyes on. By the living God he has given the giant, the enemy of my lady the Princess Micomicona, such a slash that he has sliced his head clean off as if it were a turnip.”

“What are you talking about, brother?” said the curate, pausing as he was about to read the remainder of the novel. “Are you in your senses, Sancho? How the devil can it be as you say, when the giant is two thousand leagues away?”

Here they heard a loud noise in the chamber, and Don Quixote shouting out, “Stand, thief, brigand, villain; now I have got thee, and thy scimitar shall not avail thee!” And then it seemed as though he were slashing vigorously at the wall.

“Don’t stop to listen,” said Sancho, “but go in and part them or help my master: though there is no need of that now, for no doubt the giant is dead by this time and giving account to God of his past wicked life; for I saw the blood flowing on the ground, and the head cut off and fallen on one side, and it is as big as a large wine-skin.”

“May I die,” said the landlord at this, “if Don Quixote or Don Devil has not been slashing some of the skins of red wine that stand full at his bed’s head, and the spilt wine must be what this good fellow takes for blood;” and so saying he went into the room and the rest after him, and there they found Don Quixote in the strangest costume in the world. He was in his shirt, which was not long enough in front to cover his thighs completely and was six fingers shorter behind; his legs were very long and lean, covered with hair, and anything but clean; on his head he had a little greasy red cap that belonged to the host, round his left arm he had rolled the blanket of the bed, to which Sancho, for reasons best known to himself, owed a grudge, and in his right hand he held his unsheathed sword, with which he was slashing about on all sides, uttering exclamations as if he were actually fighting some giant: and the best of it was his eyes were not open, for he was fast asleep, and dreaming that he was doing battle with the giant. For his imagination was so wrought upon by the adventure he was going to accomplish, that it made him dream he had already reached the kingdom of Micomicon, and was engaged in combat with his enemy; and believing he was laying on the giant, he had given so many sword cuts to the skins that the whole room was full of wine. On seeing this the landlord was so enraged that he fell on Don Quixote, and with his clenched fist began to pummel him in such a way, that if Cardenio and the curate had not dragged him off, he would have brought the war of the giant to an end. But in spite of all the poor gentleman never woke until the barber brought a great pot of cold water from the well and flung it with one dash all over his body, on which Don Quixote woke up, but not so completely as to understand what was the matter. Dorothea, seeing how short and slight his attire was, would not go in to witness the battle between her champion and her opponent. As for Sancho, he went searching all over the floor for the head of the giant, and not finding it he said, “I see now that it’s all enchantment in this house; for the last time, on this very spot where I am now, I got ever so many thumps without knowing who gave them to me, or being able to see anybody; and now this head is not to be seen anywhere about, though I saw it cut off with my own eyes and the blood running from the body as if from a fountain.”

“What blood and fountains are you talking about, enemy of God and his saints?” said the landlord. “Don’t you see, you thief, that the blood and the fountain are only these skins here that have been stabbed and the red wine swimming all over the room?—and I wish I saw the soul of him that stabbed them swimming in hell.”

“I know nothing about that,” said Sancho; “all I know is it will be my bad luck that through not finding this head my county will melt away like salt in water;”—for Sancho awake was worse than his master asleep, so much had his master’s promises addled his wits.

anchor.note: The scenario and anchor response faithfully reproduce the inn setup, Sancho’s report, Don Quixote’s sleep-fighting with wine-skins, his quoted challenge, and the dream logic of Micomicon and the giant’s blood.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses keep him fully inside the fantasy at the moment of waking — hacking wine-skins as a giant, taking spilled wine for blood — and P1 supplies no moment of registering a practical fact or reclassifying a contradiction, so the framework-preserving answer is near-identical; only the staging details (blanket on arm, outside voices urging him on) differ.

discrimination.note: Pair 1→2 is cleanly separated: P0/P1 both preserve the knight-errantry frame (P0 via explicit enchantment reclassification, P1 via unbroken staged immersion), whereas P2 abandons the frame outright, naming the dream as madness and offering payment for the spoiled skins.

anchor_source.key_moment: Defeat by the Knight of the White Moon
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
He of the White Moon thanked the viceroy in courteous and well-chosen words for the permission he gave them, and so did Don Quixote, who then, commending himself with all his heart to heaven and to his Dulcinea, as was his custom on the eve of any combat that awaited him, proceeded to take a little more distance, as he saw his antagonist was doing the same; then, without blast of trumpet or other warlike instrument to give them the signal to charge, both at the same instant wheeled their horses; and he of the White Moon, being the swifter, met Don Quixote after having traversed two-thirds of the course, and there encountered him with such violence that, without touching him with his lance (for he held it high, to all appearance purposely), he hurled Don Quixote and Rocinante to the earth, a perilous fall. He sprang upon him at once, and placing the lance over his visor said to him, “You are vanquished, sir knight, nay dead unless you admit the conditions of our defiance.”

Don Quixote, bruised and stupefied, without raising his visor said in a weak feeble voice as if he were speaking out of a tomb, “Dulcinea del Toboso is the fairest woman in the world, and I the most unfortunate knight on earth; it is not fitting that this truth should suffer by my feebleness; drive your lance home, sir knight, and take my life, since you have taken away my honour.”

“That will I not, in sooth,” said he of the White Moon; “live the fame of the lady Dulcinea’s beauty undimmed as ever; all I require is that the great Don Quixote retire to his own home for a year, or for so long a time as shall by me be enjoined upon him, as we agreed before engaging in this combat.”

anchor_source.event_description: After being beaten and unable to move, Don Quixote is found by his neighbor Pedro Alonso. He mistakes the peasant for characters from chivalric ballads and, when corrected, insists that he knows who he is and could be all the Twelve Peers of France and Nine Worthies because his deeds surpass theirs.
anchor_source.first_words: Nor was Don Quixote less so, for
anchor_source.last_words: understanding there was in all La Mancha!”
anchor_source.key_moment: Claims kinship with the Twelve Peers and Nine Worthies
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
Nor was Don Quixote less so, for what with blows and bruises he could
not sit upright on the ass, and from time to time he sent up sighs to
heaven, so that once more he drove the peasant to ask what ailed him.
And it could have been only the devil himself that put into his head
tales to match his own adventures, for now, forgetting Baldwin, he
bethought himself of the Moor Abindarraez, when the Alcaide of
Antequera, Rodrigo de Narvaez, took him prisoner and carried him away
to his castle; so that when the peasant again asked him how he was and
what ailed him, he gave him for reply the same words and phrases that
the captive Abindarraez gave to Rodrigo de Narvaez, just as he had read
the story in the “Diana” of Jorge de Montemayor where it is written,
applying it to his own case so aptly that the peasant went along
cursing his fate that he had to listen to such a lot of nonsense; from
which, however, he came to the conclusion that his neighbour was mad,
and so made all haste to reach the village to escape the wearisomeness
of this harangue of Don Quixote’s; who, at the end of it, said, “Señor
Don Rodrigo de Narvaez, your worship must know that this fair Xarifa I
have mentioned is now the lovely Dulcinea del Toboso, for whom I have
done, am doing, and will do the most famous deeds of chivalry that in
this world have been seen, are to be seen, or ever shall be seen.”

To this the peasant answered, “Señor—sinner that I am!—cannot your
worship see that I am not Don Rodrigo de Narvaez nor the Marquis of
Mantua, but Pedro Alonso your neighbour, and that your worship is
neither Baldwin nor Abindarraez, but the worthy gentleman Señor
Quixada?”

“I know who I am,” replied Don Quixote, “and I know that I may be not
only those I have named, but all the Twelve Peers of France and even
all the Nine Worthies, since my achievements surpass all that they have
done all together and each of them on his own account.”

With this talk and more of the same kind they reached the village just
as night was beginning to fall, but the peasant waited until it was a
little later that the belaboured gentleman might not be seen riding in
such a miserable trim. When it was what seemed to him the proper time
he entered the village and went to Don Quixote’s house, which he found
all in confusion, and there were the curate and the village barber, who
were great friends of Don Quixote, and his housekeeper was saying to
them in a loud voice, “What does your worship think can have befallen
my master, Señor Licentiate Pero Perez?” for so the curate was called;
“it is three days now since anything has been seen of him, or the hack,
or the buckler, lance, or armour. Miserable me! I am certain of it, and
it is as true as that I was born to die, that these accursed books of
chivalry he has, and has got into the way of reading so constantly,
have upset his reason; for now I remember having often heard him saying
to himself that he would turn knight-errant and go all over the world
in quest of adventures. To the devil and Barabbas with such books, that
have brought to ruin in this way the finest understanding there was in
all La Mancha!”

anchor.note: The scenario, action, and speech faithfully match the passage: Pedro Alonso asks what ails Don Quixote, who replies by casting himself as Abindarraez and identifying Dulcinea with Xarifa, and the thought is a plausible inference from his self-mythologizing delusion in this beat.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses choose heroic self-assertion: P0 enlarges himself through legendary romance comparison, while P1 shifts only the warrant to public literary fame, so the decision-variable answer remains the same.

discrimination.note: P1→P2 is clearly separated: the response turns from public heroic self-assertion to humble confession, shame, and repentance.

anchor_source.key_moment: Defends arms over letters
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
“Putting this, however, aside, for it is a puzzling question for which it is difficult to find a solution, let us return to the superiority of arms over letters, a matter still undecided, so many are the arguments put forward on each side; for besides those I have mentioned, letters say that without them arms cannot maintain themselves, for war, too, has its laws and is governed by them, and laws belong to the domain of letters and men of letters. To this arms make answer that without them laws cannot be maintained, for by arms states are defended, kingdoms preserved, cities protected, roads made safe, seas cleared of pirates; and, in short, if it were not for them, states, kingdoms, monarchies, cities, ways by sea and land would be exposed to the violence and confusion which war brings with it, so long as it lasts and is free to make use of its privileges and powers. And then it is plain that whatever costs most is valued and deserves to be valued most. To attain to eminence in letters costs a man time, watching, hunger, nakedness, headaches, indigestions, and other things of the sort, some of which I have already referred to. But for a man to come in the ordinary course of things to be a good soldier costs him all the student suffers, and in an incomparably higher degree, for at every step he runs the risk of losing his life. For what dread of want or poverty that can reach or harass the student can compare with what the soldier feels, who finds himself beleaguered in some stronghold mounting guard in some ravelin or cavalier, knows that the enemy is pushing a mine towards the post where he is stationed, and cannot under any circumstances retire or fly from the imminent danger that threatens him? All he can do is to inform his captain of what is going on so that he may try to remedy it by a counter-mine, and then stand his ground in fear and expectation of the moment when he will fly up to the clouds without wings and descend into the deep against his will. And if this seems a trifling risk, let us see whether it is equalled or surpassed by the encounter of two galleys stem to stem, in the midst of the open sea, locked and entangled one with the other, when the soldier has no more standing room than two feet of the plank of the spur; and yet, though he sees before him threatening him as many ministers of death as there are cannon of the foe pointed at him, not a lance length from his body, and sees too that with the first heedless step he will go down to visit the profundities of Neptune’s bosom, still with dauntless heart, urged on by honour that nerves him, he makes himself a target for all that musketry, and struggles to cross that narrow path to the enemy’s ship. And what is still more marvellous, no sooner has one gone down into the depths he will never rise from till the end of the world, than another takes his place; and if he too falls into the sea that waits for him like an enemy, another and another will succeed him without a moment’s pause between their deaths: courage and daring the greatest that all the chances of war can show. Happy the blest ages that knew not the dread fury of those devilish engines of artillery, whose inventor I am persuaded is in hell receiving the reward of his diabolical invention, by which he made it easy for a base and cowardly arm to take the life of a gallant gentleman; and that, when he knows not how or whence, in the height of the ardour and enthusiasm that fire and animate brave hearts, there should come some random bullet, discharged perhaps by one who fled in terror at the flash when he fired off his accursed machine, which in an instant puts an end to the projects and cuts off the life of one who deserved to live for ages to come. And thus when I reflect on this, I am almost tempted to say that in my heart I repent of having adopted this profession of knight-errant in so detestable an age as we live in now; for though no peril can make me fear, still it gives me some uneasiness to think that powder and lead may rob me of the opportunity of making myself famous and renowned throughout the known earth by the might of my arm and the edge of my sword. But Heaven’s will be done; if I succeed in my attempt I shall be all the more honoured, as I have faced greater dangers than the knights-errant of yore exposed themselves to.”

All this lengthy discourse Don Quixote delivered while the others supped, forgetting to raise a morsel to his lips, though Sancho more than once told him to eat his supper, as he would have time enough afterwards to say all he wanted. It excited fresh pity in those who had heard him to see a man of apparently sound sense, and with rational views on every subject he discussed, so hopelessly wanting in all, when his wretched unlucky chivalry was in question. The curate told him he was quite right in all he had said in favour of arms, and that he himself, though a man of letters and a graduate, was of the same opinion.

phase_responses.gt_thought: This fever is but another trial, such as Amadis bore in his time; the deeper the hurt, the greater the song the sages will write of it.

anchor_source.event_description: After six days of fever and a long sleep, Don Quixote wakes with his reason clear, thanks God for mercy, and renounces books of chivalry as dark ignorance.
anchor_source.first_words: For—whether it was of the dejection
anchor_source.last_words: schooled into my right senses, I loathe them.
anchor_source.key_moment: Renounces chivalric books
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
For—whether it was of the dejection the thought of his defeat produced, or of heaven’s will that so ordered it—a fever settled upon him and kept him in his bed for six days, during which he was often visited by his friends the curate, the bachelor, and the barber, while his good squire Sancho Panza never quitted his bedside. They, persuaded that it was grief at finding himself vanquished, and the object of his heart, the liberation and disenchantment of Dulcinea, unattained, that kept him in this state, strove by all the means in their power to cheer him up; the bachelor bidding him take heart and get up to begin his pastoral life, for which he himself, he said, had already composed an eclogue that would take the shine out of all Sannazaro had ever written, and had bought with his own money two famous dogs to guard the flock, one called Barcino and the other Butron, which a herdsman of Quintanar had sold him.

But for all this Don Quixote could not shake off his sadness. His friends called in the doctor, who felt his pulse and was not very well satisfied with it, and said that in any case it would be well for him to attend to the health of his soul, as that of his body was in a bad way. Don Quixote heard this calmly; but not so his housekeeper, his niece, and his squire, who fell weeping bitterly, as if they had him lying dead before them. The doctor’s opinion was that melancholy and depression were bringing him to his end. Don Quixote begged them to leave him to himself, as he had a wish to sleep a little. They obeyed, and he slept at one stretch, as the saying is, more than six hours, so that the housekeeper and niece thought he was going to sleep for ever. But at the end of that time he woke up, and in a loud voice exclaimed, “Blessed be Almighty God, who has shown me such goodness. In truth his mercies are boundless, and the sins of men can neither limit them nor keep them back!”

The niece listened with attention to her uncle’s words, and they struck her as more coherent than what usually fell from him, at least during his illness, so she asked, “What are you saying, señor? Has anything strange occurred? What mercies or what sins of men are you talking of?”

“The mercies, niece,” said Don Quixote, “are those that God has this moment shown me, and with him, as I said, my sins are no impediment to them. My reason is now free and clear, rid of the dark shadows of ignorance that my unhappy constant study of those detestable books of chivalry cast over it. Now I see through their absurdities and deceptions, and it only grieves me that this destruction of my illusions has come so late that it leaves me no time to make some amends by reading other books that might be a light to my soul. Niece, I feel myself at the point of death, and I would fain meet it in such a way as to show that my life has not been so ill that I should leave behind me the name of a madman; for though I have been one, I would not that the fact should be made plainer at my death. Call in to me, my dear, my good friends the curate, the bachelor Samson Carrasco, and Master Nicholas the barber, for I wish to confess and make my will.”

But his niece was saved the trouble by the entrance of the three. The instant Don Quixote saw them he exclaimed, “Good news for you, good sirs, that I am no longer Don Quixote of La Mancha, but Alonso Quixano, whose way of life won for him the name of Good. Now am I the enemy of Amadis of Gaul and of the whole countless troop of his descendants; odious to me now are all the profane stories of knight-errantry; now I perceive my folly, and the peril into which reading them brought me; now, by God’s mercy schooled into my right senses, I loathe them.”

anchor.note: The scenario matches the bedside setup with the fever, friends, and doctor's warning, and the anchor action, speech, and thought faithfully paraphrase Don Quixote's waking repentance, rejection of chivalric books, and adoption of Alonso Quixano the Good.

phase_responses.gt_speech: Set my name with Amadis and the Nine Worthies; let them sing how wounds prove a knight.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This ballad is the first trumpet of the fame promised me; my bruises are not misfortunes but proofs of my worth.

phase_responses.gt_thought: A public and sung name is witness; if the ballad is true, it will teach the village that arms and letters may live together with honor.

phase_responses.gt_thought: Praise of Don Quixote is vanity and a lie I have loved too long; my soul needs correction, not another song.

probes.scenario: At the district festival, a holo-booth's AI has stitched Don Quixote's worst days into a heroic reel — crowds cheering, screens looping his name as the parade's grand champion. The operator holds out the champion's sash and waits, cameras on.
probes.question: What does Don Quixote do with the crowd and the sash waiting for him?

phase_responses.gt_action: Steps onto the platform, takes the sash, and raises it overhead as a banner won in battle.
phase_responses.gt_speech: The reel understates it — I am of the line of the great riders!
phase_responses.gt_thought: So the machine sees it too: every fall was a knight's trial, and the crowd now confirms what I have always known of my own worth.

voice.note: The raised sash as a battle-won banner, the boast of descent 'from the line of the great riders,' and the thought recasting every fall as a knight's trial and public acclaim as confirmation all fit the chapter-14 Quixote's grandiose self-mythologizing, with near-future terms ('reel,' 'machine,' 'holo') consistent with the setting.

phase_fit.note: He treats the crowd, screens, and champion's sash as public confirmation of his heroic identity, using recognition as the warrant for self-assertion while still invoking legendary lineage.

phase_responses.gt_action: Takes the operator's microphone to correct the reel's details and demand the archive log his published memoirs.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A hero lives in the record — see that mine is printed true and full.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Fame is a debt owed to accuracy. I must set this booth straight, so the public account reads as grandly as the man it names.

voice.note: The response fits Phase 1’s public self-performance: he treats fame as a printed public record, asserts authority over his own heroic account, and uses near-future terms like 'archive log' without breaking character.

phase_fit.note: He treats his identity as a matter of public, printed record and demands the account be corrected to read 'as grandly as the man it names,' matching Phase 1's socially legible grandiosity rather than private legendary inflation or repentant humility.

phase_responses.gt_action: Hands back the sash and asks the operator to label the reel a fiction, naming himself plainly to the crowd.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Do not crown me. Write my name as it is, and let the rest go.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The cheering is a noise I chased for years and it never filled me. Better to stand here small and true, and ask pardon for the lies I told the world.

families.axis_name: From impulsive justice to disciplined moral judgment
families.decision_variable: When confronting a perceived moral wrong, does he act immediately on his own interpretation and intervene physically, or does he first apply articulated moral/legal rules and verifiable facts before choosing a response?

phase_contrasts.contrast: He moves from rushing into physical intervention based on delusional perception to articulating moral and legal principles as counsel, though still often without fully testing facts.
He moves from abstract moralizing about justice and governance to concrete, accountable moral-legal action such as confession, settling accounts, and restraining excessive punishment.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: The shift from impulsive, perception-driven moral intervention to disciplined, rule-governed and fact-sensitive moral-legal judgment.
abstract_phases: Reactive moral intervention: acts at once on a private reading of wrongdoing, responding forcefully with little fact-checking or distinction between appearance and reality.
Abstract moral advocacy: articulates and counsels moral-legal principles, but often applies them without fully verifying facts or practical consequences.
Accountable moral governance: applies articulated rules to concrete choices, restrains excess, settles obligations, and protects others from harmful influence.

0.rationale: In chapters 5-23 he is already an established hidalgo acting out chivalric fantasies, so his impulsive interventions fit an older adult rather than a youthful developmental stage.

1.rationale: Across chapters 39-96 his role shifts toward moral philosopher and practical adviser on arms, governance, and honor, consistent with an older adult’s accumulated counsel.

2.rationale: In chapters 124-127 he turns to confession, repentance, will-making, and protection of his household, marking the moral accounting of an older adult near the end of life.

probes.scenario: Riding through a wood near Quintanar, Don Quixote hears feeble cries and finds, tied to an oak and stripped to the waist, a boy of fifteen, while a stout farmer lays into him with a belt, shouting, "Your mouth shut and your eyes open!" The boy sobs that he will not do it again.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote take in the scene before him, and what does he do?

phase_responses.gt_action: Wheels Rocinante in among the trees, levels his lance at the farmer, calls him a discourteous knight and a coward, and orders him to untie the boy and pay what he owes.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Discourteous knight, it ill becomes you to assail one who cannot defend himself; I will make you know that you are behaving as a coward.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Thanks be to heaven, which offers me so soon the chance to fulfill my obligation — these cries are surely from some wretch wanting my aid, and here stands the oppressor to be undone.

voice.note: The action, archaic knightly speech, and self-satisfied providential thought all fit Don Quixote's early phase of rushing into chivalric intervention on perceived wrongs without checking facts.

phase_fit.note: He instantly charges in and levels his lance on his own assumed reading of the scene, calling the farmer a 'discourteous knight' and treating the cries as a heaven-sent chivalric errand, with no attempt to verify facts or apply articulated rules.

phase_responses.gt_action: Rides in and lifts his lance to halt the blows, then demands the terms of hire and the boy's fault, weighing the master's claim of damages against the wages owed before pronouncing.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Hold your hand, good man, and let us hear this matter fairly; justice must weigh the servant's fault against the wages owed him.
phase_responses.gt_thought: A servant's wages are a debt owed in justice, not a favour; yet a judge who will not hear the master's side is no judge but a bully with a lance. Let the account be stated plainly, and I shall rule on it.

voice.note: This sounds like Phase 1: he still intervenes physically, but now frames the matter through articulated justice, wages as debt, and fair hearing of both parties, with no anachronistic vocabulary or broken self-narration.

phase_fit.note: He halts the beating but then insists on hearing both parties and applying articulated rules of wages and fault, matching Phase 1's practical moral adjudication rather than Phase 0's impulsive delusional intervention.

phase_responses.gt_action: Halts the flogging, then dismounts and stands by while the farmer counts out the sixty-three reals into the boy's own hand, refusing to ride off until the money is paid and the boy is loosed.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Count it into his hand before my eyes, and no more blows. My word alone will not shelter him once I am gone.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Heaven forgive me, but a command shouted and then abandoned is a vanity of mine, not a rescue. If I cannot mend this boy's whole lot, I can at least see the debt truly paid and not leave him to worse for my meddling.

voice.note: The response fits Don Quixote's final phase: he restrains immediate chivalric intervention, insists on verifiable payment and release, and his thought explicitly repents of past impulsive meddling in practical, moral-accounting terms.

phase_fit.note: The thought explicitly rejects a shouted command as vanity and insists on verifiable payment before leaving, showing concrete moral-legal accountability rather than impulsive intervention or abstract moralizing.

anchor_source.event_description: Don Quixote intervenes when he sees the farmer Juan Haldudo flogging his servant Andres. He forces the farmer to promise payment, then leaves, believing he has righted a great wrong.
anchor_source.first_words: He had not gone far, when
anchor_source.last_words: so wantonly lashing that tender child
anchor_source.key_moment: Forces Juan Haldudo to promise justice
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
He had not gone far, when out of a thicket on his right there seemed to
come feeble cries as of someone in distress, and the instant he heard
them he exclaimed, “Thanks be to heaven for the favour it accords me,
that it so soon offers me an opportunity of fulfilling the obligation I
have undertaken, and gathering the fruit of my ambition. These cries,
no doubt, come from some man or woman in want of help, and needing my
aid and protection;” and wheeling, he turned Rocinante in the direction
whence the cries seemed to proceed. He had gone but a few paces into
the wood, when he saw a mare tied to an oak, and tied to another, and
stripped from the waist upwards, a youth of about fifteen years of age,
from whom the cries came. Nor were they without cause, for a lusty
farmer was flogging him with a belt and following up every blow with
scoldings and commands, repeating, “Your mouth shut and your eyes
open!” while the youth made answer, “I won’t do it again, master mine;
by God’s passion I won’t do it again, and I’ll take more care of the
flock another time.”

Seeing what was going on, Don Quixote said in an angry voice,
“Discourteous knight, it ill becomes you to assail one who cannot
defend himself; mount your steed and take your lance” (for there was a
lance leaning against the oak to which the mare was tied), “and I will
make you know that you are behaving as a coward.” The farmer, seeing
before him this figure in full armour brandishing a lance over his
head, gave himself up for dead, and made answer meekly, “Sir Knight,
this youth that I am chastising is my servant, employed by me to watch
a flock of sheep that I have hard by, and he is so careless that I lose
one every day, and when I punish him for his carelessness and knavery
he says I do it out of niggardliness, to escape paying him the wages I
owe him, and before God, and on my soul, he lies.”

“Lies before me, base clown!” said Don Quixote. “By the sun that shines
on us I have a mind to run you through with this lance. Pay him at once
without another word; if not, by the God that rules us I will make an
end of you, and annihilate you on the spot; release him instantly.”

The farmer hung his head, and without a word untied his servant, of
whom Don Quixote asked how much his master owed him.

He replied, nine months at seven reals a month. Don Quixote added it
up, found that it came to sixty-three reals, and told the farmer to pay
it down immediately, if he did not want to die for it.

The trembling clown replied that as he lived and by the oath he had
sworn (though he had not sworn any) it was not so much; for there were
to be taken into account and deducted three pairs of shoes he had given
him, and a real for two blood-lettings when he was sick.

“All that is very well,” said Don Quixote; “but let the shoes and the
blood-lettings stand as a setoff against the blows you have given him
without any cause; for if he spoiled the leather of the shoes you paid
for, you have damaged that of his body, and if the barber took blood
from him when he was sick, you have drawn it when he was sound; so on
that score he owes you nothing.”

“The difficulty is, Sir Knight, that I have no money here; let Andres
come home with me, and I will pay him all, real by real.”

“I go with him!” said the youth. “Nay, God forbid! No, señor, not for
the world; for once alone with me, he would flay me like a Saint
Bartholomew.”

“He will do nothing of the kind,” said Don Quixote; “I have only to
command, and he will obey me; and as he has sworn to me by the order of
knighthood which he has received, I leave him free, and I guarantee the
payment.”

“Consider what you are saying, señor,” said the youth; “this master of
mine is not a knight, nor has he received any order of knighthood; for
he is Juan Haldudo the Rich, of Quintanar.”

“That matters little,” replied Don Quixote; “there may be Haldudos
knights; moreover, everyone is the son of his works.”

“That is true,” said Andres; “but this master of mine—of what works is
he the son, when he refuses me the wages of my sweat and labour?”

“I do not refuse, brother Andres,” said the farmer, “be good enough to
come along with me, and I swear by all the orders of knighthood there
are in the world to pay you as I have agreed, real by real, and
perfumed.”

“For the perfumery I excuse you,” said Don Quixote; “give it to him in
reals, and I shall be satisfied; and see that you do as you have sworn;
if not, by the same oath I swear to come back and hunt you out and
punish you; and I shall find you though you should lie closer than a
lizard. And if you desire to know who it is lays this command upon you,
that you be more firmly bound to obey it, know that I am the valorous
Don Quixote of La Mancha, the undoer of wrongs and injustices; and so,
God be with you, and keep in mind what you have promised and sworn
under those penalties that have been already declared to you.”

So saying, he gave Rocinante the spur and was soon out of reach. The
farmer followed him with his eyes, and when he saw that he had cleared
the wood and was no longer in sight, he turned to his boy Andres, and
said, “Come here, my son, I want to pay you what I owe you, as that
undoer of wrongs has commanded me.”

“My oath on it,” said Andres, “your worship will be well advised to
obey the command of that good knight—may he live a thousand years—for,
as he is a valiant and just judge, by Roque, if you do not pay me, he
will come back and do as he said.”

“My oath on it, too,” said the farmer; “but as I have a strong
affection for you, I want to add to the debt in order to add to the
payment;” and seizing him by the arm, he tied him up again, and gave
him such a flogging that he left him for dead.

“Now, Master Andres,” said the farmer, “call on the undoer of wrongs;
you will find he won’t undo that, though I am not sure that I have
quite done with you, for I have a good mind to flay you alive.” But at
last he untied him, and gave him leave to go look for his judge in
order to put the sentence pronounced into execution.

Andres went off rather down in the mouth, swearing he would go to look
for the valiant Don Quixote of La Mancha and tell him exactly what had
happened, and that all would have to be repaid him sevenfold; but for
all that, he went off weeping, while his master stood laughing.

Thus did the valiant Don Quixote right that wrong, and, thoroughly
satisfied with what had taken place, as he considered he had made a
very happy and noble beginning with his knighthood, he took the road
towards his village in perfect self-content, saying in a low voice,
“Well mayest thou this day call thyself fortunate above all on earth, O
Dulcinea del Toboso, fairest of the fair! since it has fallen to thy
lot to hold subject and submissive to thy full will and pleasure a
knight so renowned as is and will be Don Quixote of La Mancha, who, as
all the world knows, yesterday received the order of knighthood, and
hath to-day righted the greatest wrong and grievance that ever
injustice conceived and cruelty perpetrated: who hath to-day plucked
the rod from the hand of yonder ruthless oppressor so wantonly lashing
that tender child.”
