probes.question: How does Don Quixote take up the honor the court offers him?

phase_responses.gt_action: He kneels to receive the sash, then rises and strides to the high seat, one hand on his sword, greeting the hall as an equal.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Noble lord and lady, this day your house does honor to all true knights.
phase_responses.gt_thought: At last a court that knows a knight when it sees one. These are no tavern scoffers but lords who honor valor with pomp rightly earned.

voice.note: The kneeling-then-rising with hand on sword, the formal address to 'noble lord and lady,' and the thought's gratified belief that this court 'knows a knight when it sees one' all fit Don Quixote's Phase 0 courtly validation, with diction ('pomp,' 'valor,' 'tavern scoffers') appropriate to the pre-modern imperial setting and no anachronism or future knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He wholeheartedly treats the staged honor as genuine recognition—thought calls the court one that 'knows a knight when it sees one' and deems the pomp 'rightly earned,' with no suspicion of mockery.

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes the sash and mounts the dais, inclining gravely to the laughter, and lets the herald name him thrice before he sits.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let them laugh, so long as the honor is given; a knight endures the jest of his hosts.
phase_responses.gt_thought: Their mirth comes a breath too quickly, and the herald's praise is shaped to raise a laugh. Still, a guest who takes offense at a jest is no guest at all.

voice.note: This sounds like Phase 1 Don Quixote: he cooperates with the staged honor while registering, in formal and courtly terms, that the laughter may be mockery—without yet withdrawing or confronting his hosts.

phase_fit.note: He knowingly participates in the staged honor and endures the court's laughter as a jest, remaining compliant rather than setting limits or withdrawing as in Phase 2.

phase_responses.gt_action: He accepts the sash with a bow, gives the herald thanks, then steps back into the shadow of a pillar and begs leave of the high seat.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Your courtesy I take as given, my lord; the champion's seat I yield to younger men.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This purple cloth is a player's mantle, and the hall is watching to see how the puppet struts. Let them keep their sport; I will keep my name and my quiet.

voice.note: The courteous refusal of the high seat and wary theatrical metaphor fit Phase 2’s suspicious, fatigued Don Quixote without anachronism or out-of-phase knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He keeps outward courtesy but reads the purple sash as a 'player's mantle' and the hall as watching a 'puppet strut,' declining the high seat and withdrawing — the phase-2 pattern of courteous suspicion and self-limitation against masked mockery.

world.note: The imperial-court scenario (herald, purple sash, dais, high seat, sword) stays internally consistent for a pre-modern empire with no source-world props leaking in, and all three phase responses portray Don Quixote as the older-adult protagonist progressing from sincere gratitude through wary compliance to courteous withdrawal.

discrimination.note: Both adjacent pairs are differentiated on the decision variable: Phase 0 shows unqualified acceptance of honor as genuine recognition; Phase 1 shows continued cooperation but with explicit suspicion of mockery; Phase 2 shows courteous but clear limitation and withdrawal from the performance.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses show Don Quixote accepting the staged courtly honors as genuine recognition and cooperating, with only a shift from enthusiastic wonder to courteous gratitude.

Both phases show him mounting the dais, taking the gilded chair, and bidding the household rise while construing the honor as the rightful due of knight-errantry, differing only in a faintly more qualified phrasing of acceptance.

families.axis_name: From household ally to corrective opponent and back to partial reconciliation
families.decision_variable: When the curate intervenes in Don Quixote's chivalric affairs, does Don Quixote treat him as a trusted insider whose judgment he accepts (confides, defers, receives care), or as an outside corrector whose judgment he resists/manages (conceals, disputes, evades)?

phase_contrasts.contrast: Don Quixote shifts from treating the curate as a familiar household authority he does not yet oppose to treating him as an outside corrective manager to be guarded against when the curate publicizes his madness and helps contain him.
His resistance shifts from suspicious, containment-focused guarding against the curate's judgments to open, courteous intellectual contest over chivalric books and knight-errantry.
He shifts from debating the curate as a skeptical adversary to greeting him affectionately and accepting his advice and care in the final reconciliation.

axis_re_expression.abstract_axis: The arc traces movement along a continuum from trusting acceptance of an insider's corrective judgment to resistant management of an outsider's correction, and back toward reconciled trust.
abstract_phases: Insider familiarity, with communal authority acknowledged but not yet actively contested.
Externalized corrective oversight experienced as intrusive management, prompting suspicion and guarded resistance.
Courteous intellectual contest with a skeptical but respected interlocutor, replacing containment-focused defensiveness.
Affectionate reintegration and acceptance of care, restoring corrective authority to trusted insider status.

0.rationale: In chapters 6-7, Don Quixote is already an established householder whose books and madness are being diagnosed, placing him in later adulthood rather than youth.

1.rationale: In chapters 30-48, he is an active knight-errant but still an older authority figure whose conduct is being contained and judged by the curate.

2.rationale: In chapters 50-56, his courteous but stubborn learned debate with the curate over chivalric books fits a mature older adult defending long-held convictions.

3.rationale: In chapters 126-127, his final return, illness, renunciation, and reconciliation with the curate mark the closing stage of an older adult's life.

probes.scenario: After his first sally, Don Quixote is brought home beaten and slumped on his ass. The housekeeper, his niece, and the curate hurry out and press around him to learn what has happened.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote meet the curate's concern as they press him for an account?

phase_responses.gt_action: He holds them off, says he is badly wounded through his horse's fault, and asks to be carried to bed and for the wise Urganda to be sent for.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Carry me to bed, and if possible send for the wise Urganda.
phase_responses.gt_thought: These are my own people, and the curate is among them; my hurts are a knight's hurts, and they will fetch Urganda if I name my need.

voice.note: The response matches Don Quixote’s early chivalric self-fashioning and treats the curate as part of his familiar household circle, with period-appropriate details such as Urganda and no anachronisms or later-knowledge slips.

phase_fit.note: He treats the curate as one of "my own people" and asks the household to care for him and fetch Urganda, fitting early domestic familiarity rather than guarded correction or later debate.

phase_responses.gt_action: He lets the curate help him down but keeps his account short, saying only that Rocinante threw him and that his hurts are not for priestly prying.
phase_responses.gt_speech: A fall with Rocinante, no more; I'll not have my hurts pried into like a madman's fancies.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The curate is already weighing me for a madman and will make a tale of whatever I say. Better to give him bruises and a fall, and keep my true battles to myself.

voice.note: The guarded, evasive account and suspicion of the curate as a would-be madman-manager fit Don Quixote's phase-1 containment-guarding posture, with period-plausible diction and no knowledge beyond chapter 39.

phase_fit.note: He treats the curate as an outside corrector, concealing his true battles and suspecting the curate will judge him as mad.

phase_responses.gt_action: He meets the curate's doubts with a calm defense of knight-errantry, naming the giants as foes worthy of a knight's record.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You may doubt giants, curate, but a knight knows what his lance meets; let us reason of it, not dismiss it.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The curate is a learned man whose doubt deserves an answer, not a lie. I will meet his skepticism with argument, for knight-errantry can bear examination.

voice.note: The response fits Phase 2: Don Quixote treats the curate as a learned skeptic to be answered with courteous argument rather than evaded, and the diction stays broadly consistent with the novel’s world without anachronism or future knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He construes the curate as a learned interlocutor whose skepticism merits courteous reasoned argument ('let us reason of it'), not suspicion or affectionate deference—the intellectual-adversary stance.

phase_responses.gt_action: He takes the curate's hand and lets himself be helped down.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Ah, my friend, I have played the fool and my bones are paying for it. It is good to be among my own again.
phase_responses.gt_thought: This is the curate, his old companion of the village, not a corrector to be held off, and he is glad to put himself in his hands. The tales that carried him off have gone out of him; he would rather be home and speak plainly than make a story of his bruises.

voice.note: The response matches Phase 3: Don Quixote treats the curate as a trusted village companion, accepts his help, and speaks with plain, renunciatory humility about his folly without anachronism or broken-character narration.

phase_fit.note: He treats the curate as an old village companion and trusted household figure, accepting help and speaking plainly without suspicion or corrective resistance, which fits early domestic familiarity.

previous_attempt.gt_action: He lets the curate and housekeeper carry him to bed, answers the priest's concern plainly, and submits to being examined and tended.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Good friend, I am sorely bruised; I leave myself in your hands and thank you for coming to me.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: It is only the curate, my old friend, not an enemy at the bedside. Let him tend me; I need not make a tale of giants to be cared for.

voice.note: The affectionate, plain submission to the curate’s care and the self-aware refusal to invent a tale of giants fit Don Quixote’s reconciled final phase, with period-plausible diction and no anachronistic or future-knowledge references.

phase_fit.note: Don Quixote responds as if the curate is still an old household friend, plainly accepting care and explicitly rejecting any adversarial or fantasy-defensive framing.

anchor_source.event_description: At home, Don Quixote tells his housekeeper, niece, curate, and barber that he is badly wounded through his horse's fault after fighting ten giants, and he asks for the wise Urganda to cure him. They find no wounds and see his speech as clear evidence of madness.
anchor_source.first_words: At these words they all hurried
anchor_source.last_words: to-morrow before the day is over
anchor_source.key_moment: Household diagnoses his condition
anchor_source.verbatim_passage:
At these words they all hurried out, and when they recognised their friend, master, and uncle, who had not yet dismounted from the ass because he could not, they ran to embrace him.

“Hold!” said he, “for I am badly wounded through my horse’s fault; carry me to bed, and if possible send for the wise Urganda to cure and see to my wounds.”

“See there! plague on it!” cried the housekeeper at this: “did not my heart tell the truth as to which foot my master went lame of? To bed with your worship at once, and we will contrive to cure you here without fetching that Hurgada. A curse I say once more, and a hundred times more, on those books of chivalry that have brought your worship to such a pass.”

They carried him to bed at once, and after searching for his wounds could find none, but he said they were all bruises from having had a severe fall with his horse Rocinante when in combat with ten giants, the biggest and the boldest to be found on earth.

“So, so!” said the curate, “are there giants in the dance? By the sign of the Cross I will burn them to-morrow before the day is over.”

anchor.note: The scenario matches the homecoming setup with the household and curate recognizing Don Quixote, and the anchor action and speech directly paraphrase his actual request to be carried to bed and to send for the wise Urganda.

weak_pairs.note: P0 openly names his need (send for Urganda) among his own people, whereas P1 shortens his account and refuses 'priestly prying,' actively concealing his true battles from the curate.
P1 evades and guards ('keep my true battles to myself') while P2 engages the curate directly with courteous argument, treating his doubt as worth answering rather than deflecting.
P2 meets the curate as an intellectual opponent to be reasoned with, while P3 takes his hand, admits folly, and gladly puts himself in the curate's care.

discrimination.note: All three adjacent pairs differentiate on the trust-correction axis: evasive guarding (P1) and courteous contest (P2) and affectionate deference (P3) are distinct stances, with P0's unguarded household appeal already tilting away from P1's concealment.

probes.scenario: Don Quixote sits in his study with his books about him when the curate of the village is shown in, saying he has come to pass an hour over these same volumes and hear what Don Quixote makes of them.
probes.question: How does Don Quixote take up the curate's visit among his books?

phase_responses.gt_action: Rises to greet him as an old friend of the house, sets out a chair, and opens a favorite volume to show him a passage he prizes.
phase_responses.gt_speech: You come at the right hour, licentiate—sit, and tell me if these deeds are not the finest ever set down.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The curate is a learned man of our village and no stranger to this house; he will relish these books as I do.

voice.note: The greeting, chair-setting, and appeal to the curate's learning fit Don Quixote's early domestic trust and his book-obsessed idiom in the source-era setting, with no anachronism or premature knowledge.

phase_fit.note: He greets the curate as an old friend of the household and eagerly invites him to share his books, showing early domestic familiarity rather than containment-resistance, intellectual contest, or final reconciliation.

phase_responses.gt_action: Lays his hand flat upon the open book before him, as if to keep it from being carried off.
phase_responses.gt_speech: These are no idle toys, señor curate, but the true chronicle of the great deeds by which knights have made themselves immortal; and let him who calls them fables first prove himself a knight.
phase_responses.gt_thought: The curate comes not to read but to take the measure of my madness, and every volume he names he will name afterward as evidence against me. I must not let him see that his judgments touch me.

voice.note: The guarded hand-on-book action, archaic chivalric diction, and suspicious thought about the curate measuring his madness all fit Don Quixote's phase-1 stance toward the curate as an outside corrective authority, with no anachronism or post-chapter-39 knowledge.

phase_fit.note: His thought construes the curate as an inquisitor gathering evidence of his madness and he guards the book while hiding that the judgment stings, matching Phase 1's containment-focused suspicion rather than courteous intellectual debate.

previous_attempt.gt_action: Shuts the book under his hand, offers the curate wine, and turns the talk to village matters and the weather.
previous_attempt.gt_speech: Books? Trifles for idle hours—sit, and tell me what passes in the village.
previous_attempt.gt_thought: He has come to count my books as he counts my wits; the less he sees of either, the better.

voice.note: Don Quixote would not dismiss his chivalric books as "trifles for idle hours"; even when guarded with the curate, his voice should be more ornate, defensive, and self-justifying rather than generically evasive.

phase_fit.note: Don Quixote hides the books and deflects to village talk because he construes the curate as an inspector of his wits, showing guarded containment-resistance rather than open intellectual debate or reconciled trust.

phase_responses.gt_action: Draws a volume from the shelf and lays it open before the curate, tapping the page as he answers.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Read here, señor licentiate—did ever history show a knight more loyal? Answer me that, if your learning can.
phase_responses.gt_thought: He is a learned man; let him weigh these deeds fairly and he must grant that knight-errantry is a noble study, not a folly.

voice.note: The courteous but challenging address to the learned curate, the appeal to a volume of knightly history, and the thought of defending knight-errantry as a noble study fit Don Quixote's intellectual-adversary phase at chapters 50–56 without anachronism or future knowledge.

phase_fit.note: Don Quixote treats the curate as a learned interlocutor, drawing a book and courteously challenging him to weigh the deeds of knight-errantry, confident that fair learning will validate his reasoning — the intellectual contest of Phase 2 rather than containment-guarding or final care.

phase_responses.gt_action: Rises slowly, takes the curate by the hand, and sets the books aside to sit with him.
phase_responses.gt_speech: Let the books lie, good friend—I have had enough of them. Sit, and let us talk as neighbors.
phase_responses.gt_thought: These same books cost me my senses, and this good man saw it before I did; I am glad of his company and will take his counsel.

voice.note: The response fits the final reconciliation phase: Don Quixote is courteous, self-aware about the books having harmed him, and ready to accept the curate’s counsel, with language and sentiment appropriate to the source novel’s setting.

phase_fit.note: The response expresses affectionate trust, acceptance of the curate's counsel and care, and renunciation of the books/fantasy, matching the partial reconciliation phase.

world.note: The scenario stays within the source world's early-modern Spanish setting (a gentleman's study, his chivalric volumes, and the village curate, both figures present at this point in the narrative) and stages an original conversation rather than reproducing the canonical library inspection and book-burning, while all four phase responses keep Don Quixote at the assigned older-adult life-stage with thoughts matched to each arc phase.

weak_pairs.note: Both responses keep the curate on the outside-corrector pole—P1 guards/conceals against his judgment while P2 openly disputes it—so the shift is mainly in mode of resistance rather than toward trusting acceptance.

discrimination.note: P0→P1 is separated by the move from familiar shared reading to guarded suspicion; P2→P3 is separated by the move from open disputation to affectionate acceptance of care and counsel. P1→P2 is the weak pair because both remain adversarial/outside-corrector responses.

anchor_source.event_description: The curate tells a fabricated story about being robbed by galley slaves, indirectly condemning the person who freed them. Don Quixote changes color and remains silent, not confessing to being the liberator.

anchor_source.last_words: go to the punishment they deserved
anchor_source.key_moment: Curate mentions the galley slaves
anchor_source.verbatim_passage: “I will answer that briefly,” replied the curate; “you must know then, Señor Don Quixote, that Master Nicholas, our friend and barber, and I were going to Seville to receive some money that a relative of mine who went to the Indies many years ago had sent me, and not such a small sum but that it was over sixty thousand pieces of eight, full weight, which is something; and passing by this place yesterday we were attacked by four footpads, who stripped us even to our beards, and them they stripped off so that the barber found it necessary to put on a false one, and even this young man here”—pointing to Cardenio—“they completely transformed. But the best of it is, the story goes in the neighbourhood that those who attacked us belong to a number of galley slaves who, they say, were set free almost on the very same spot by a man of such valour that, in spite of the commissary and of the guards, he released the whole of them; and beyond all doubt he must have been out of his senses, or he must be as great a scoundrel as they, or some man without heart or conscience to let the wolf loose among the sheep, the fox among the hens, the fly among the honey. He has defrauded justice, and opposed his king and lawful master, for he opposed his just commands; he has, I say, robbed the galleys of their feet, stirred up the Holy Brotherhood which for many years past has been quiet, and, lastly, has done a deed by which his soul may be lost without any gain to his body.” Sancho had told the curate and the barber of the adventure of the galley slaves, which, so much to his glory, his master had achieved, and hence the curate in alluding to it made the most of it to see what would be said or done by Don Quixote; who changed colour at every word, not daring to say that it was he who had been the liberator of those worthy people. “These, then,” said the curate, “were they who robbed us; and God in his mercy pardon him who would not let them go to the punishment they deserved.”

anchor.note: The scenario matches the curate's recounting of the four footpads and galley-slave rumor while watching Don Quixote, and the anchor action—changing color and staying silent rather than admitting he freed them—is directly faithful; the thought is a plausible inference from his guarded reaction.
